title: AI runs its own biology lab - and stores a sentence in DNA
dek: A lab in China plans and carries out experiments with almost no human input, but people are still needed behind the scenes.

article: Scientists in China have built a laboratory that can plan and carry out its own biology experiments, with artificial intelligence (AI) making almost every decision.

The system, called AutoDNA, was developed by researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and described in the journal Nature on 4 November. A user types a single request in plain language, and the lab does the rest: it searches the scientific literature, chooses reagents, designs a procedure, writes the code that controls the machines and analyses the results.

Behind the scenes, six AI "agents" divide the work. One acts as the planner, another proposes explanations when results look poor, and others manage chemical supplies or turn instructions into code. Robotic arms then move samples between more than 20 types of instrument.

Before any real liquid is moved, the code is tested in a virtual copy of the lab. In one case, this check caught a mistake in which a machine would have tried to measure a sample that had not yet been loaded.

The most ambitious test was a DNA data-storage "round trip". Digital information was converted into a sequence of DNA letters, written into 78 synthetic DNA strands, stored, then read back by sequencing and decoded. The original sentence came back intact - but the process took 11,382 hardware steps and more than eight days.
The lab also detected a virus that affects pigs, with results statistically indistinguishable from those of human technicians, and identified a cancer-related mutation in tumour tissue.

However, the claim that no humans are needed comes with caveats. People still chose the tasks, prepared reagents, refilled supplies and cleared away waste. Of 14 hardware errors recorded, the system fixed eight on its own; humans dealt with the other six.

James Zou, a Stanford University scientist who wrote a commentary in the same issue of Nature, noted that AI can now design candidate molecules in minutes, while testing them at the bench still takes weeks or months. He described AutoDNA as a step towards closing that gap, but argued that labs will remain expensive custom builds until instrument makers agree on a common way for software to control their machines.

The researchers also acknowledge a further weakness. Because AI language models contain an element of randomness, the same request may not always produce the same procedure - a potential problem in science, where results must be reproducible. For now, the system is best suited to standardised tests rather than complex work such as experiments on animals.

tasks.q: Which headline best sums up the WHOLE article?
options: AI lab runs biology experiments almost on its own
Chinese scientists replace all lab workers with robots
DNA becomes the world's main way to store data
Stanford warns that AI labs are too dangerous
tasks.explain: B goes too far (humans are still needed). C takes one detail and exaggerates it. D twists Zou's view: he only said labs are expensive custom builds.

tasks.q: Put the DNA data-storage round trip in the right order (paragraph 5).
items: Turn digital information into a sequence of DNA letters
Write the sequence into synthetic DNA strands
Keep the DNA strands in storage
Read the strands back by sequencing
Decode the letters into the original sentence
tasks.explain: Encode → synthesise → store → sequence → decode. Words like "then" and "read back" signal the order.

tasks.q: Scan the article: what does each number refer to?

pairs.right: hardware steps in the storage test
errors that humans had to fix

tasks.explain: For numbers, don't reread everything - let your eyes jump to the digits, then read only the words around them.

statements.text: AutoDNA tests its code in a virtual lab before handling real samples.
statements.explain: Paragraph 4: the code is tested in a virtual copy of the lab before any real liquid is moved.

statements.text: The DNA storage test finished in less than a week.
statements.explain: Paragraph 5: it took more than eight days.

statements.text: AutoDNA detected the pig virus faster than human technicians.
statements.explain: Paragraph 6 compares the RESULTS (indistinguishable), not the speed. Speed is never mentioned.

statements.text: Most of the recorded hardware errors were fixed without human help.
statements.explain: Paragraph 7: 8 of the 14 were fixed by the system.

statements.text: The researchers plan to sell AutoDNA to hospitals.
statements.explain: Nothing in the article mentions selling it or hospitals.

tasks.q: According to Zou, why will autonomous labs stay expensive for now?
options: Each lab must be custom-built, because instrument makers lack a shared way for software to control machines
AI models still take weeks to design new molecules
Reagents for DNA experiments are rare and costly
The robots make too many errors that humans must fix
tasks.explain: Paragraph 8: labs remain 'expensive custom builds until instrument makers agree on a common way...'. B reverses the facts: AI designs molecules in MINUTES.

tasks.q: In paragraph 7, "the claim ... comes with caveats" is closest in meaning to:
options: the claim is true only with important limitations
the claim is widely praised by experts
the claim is protected by law
tasks.explain: The sentences that follow list the limits (humans still prepare reagents, fix errors...). Use the context after a new word to guess it.

tasks.q: Why does the writer mention "an element of randomness" in the last paragraph?
options: To point out a possible problem with repeating results
To explain why the lab is so fast
To show that the AI is creative
To prove that the experiment failed
tasks.explain: 'a further weakness' + 'results must be reproducible' tell you the purpose: it's a limitation.

write.prompt: Would you trust results from a lab run by AI? Write 2-3 sentences in English. Try to use one word from today's word list.
write.sample: I would trust the results only if they were reproducible. AutoDNA is impressive, but its claims come with caveats: humans still fix errors, and the same request may not give the same procedure.
